source: Hammond (1986) CHEF: A model of case-based planning
finding: CHEF is the founding adaptation-by-edit system. It has six processes: problem anticipation, plan retrieval, plan modification, plan repair, credit assignment, plan storage. A retrieved plan is edited to meet goals it does not yet meet, then run in simulation, and if it fails a causal explanation of the failure picks a repair strategy.
numbers: Domain: Szechwan stir-fry recipes. Worked example: a stored beef-and-broccoli plan is modified into chicken-and-snow-peas by substituting chicken for beef and snow pea for broccoli. A plan in the domain has about 17 steps over a dozen ingredients. No benchmark percentages; demonstration by worked examples.
quote: Successful plans are stored in memory, indexed by the goals they satisfy and the problems they avoid.
limits: Single worked example; no controlled evaluation; hand-built domain knowledge for repair and critics. Cooking domain is small.
agent_relevance: Maps directly to O7: retrieve a stored solution, edit it by named substitutions, test it, and on failure explain the failure before repairing. The explain-then-repair order matches guardrail G2.

source: Hammond (1986) CHEF: A model of case-based planning (modification step)
finding: Modification uses ingredient-specific critics. When an ingredient is swapped, the critic of the new ingredient adds steps the old one did not need (example: bone the chicken before chopping) and removes steps tied to the old item.
numbers: Example trace: 'Substituting chicken for beef in new plan'; 'Substituting snow pea for broccoli'; critic adds 'Bone the chicken' before 'Chop the chicken'.
quote: Before doing step: Chop the chicken ... do: Bone the chicken. - Critic applied.
limits: Critics are hand-written per ingredient; CHEF does not learn them.
agent_relevance: A substitution edit must be followed by a check for side-effect steps that the new item needs. In a scaffold this is a post-edit consequences pass, but the consequences should be checked by running, not by model opinion (G2, G3).

source: Hammond (1986) CHEF: A model of case-based planning (anticipation and failure memory)
finding: CHEF stores failures indexed by the goal features that interacted to cause them (beef plus crisp vegetable gives soggy broccoli). On a new plan with the same goal features it predicts the failure BEFORE building the plan and retrieves a plan that already avoids it, so it does not recreate and debug old mistakes.
numbers: Failure example: liquid from stir-fried beef made broccoli soggy; the failure is indexed by the interacting goals, not by surface features of the dish.
quote: Memories of past failures are used to warn the planner of impending problems
limits: Indexing by goal interaction is hand-coded. Only one failure family shown.
agent_relevance: Store failed edits with the cause, indexed by what interacted. Before editing a retrieved solution, check whether a stored failure matches the new situation (supports O7 and retention of failure cases).

source: Ye, Zhao, Leake, Wang, Crandall (2021) Applying the Case Difference Heuristic to Learn Adaptations from Deep Network Features (DL-CDH)
finding: The case difference heuristic (CDH, Hanney and Keane 1996) learns adaptation from pairs of cases: the problem difference becomes the rule condition, the solution difference becomes the action. DL-CDH trains a network on features from a pretrained CNN to predict the age difference between two faces, then adds that difference to the retrieved case's age.
numbers: IMDB-WIKI faces, 22,578 images after filtering, VGG-Face features of 2622 dims. Normal setting, mean error in years: constant 12.94, regressor 5.97, L1 retrieve 9.58 then adapt 8.14, Siamese retrieve 7.49 then adapt 7.86.
quote: The CBR system achieves slightly lower performance overall than a baseline deep network regressor, but better performance than the baseline on novel queries.
limits: Regression on one image task. Authors state adaptation can make Siamese retrieval WORSE in-distribution (7.49 to 7.86) because retrieval and adaptation are trained separately.
agent_relevance: Adaptation by learned difference is not free: an edit step can lower quality if the retrieved case was already very close. Keep the 'no edit' option and compare edited against unedited with a check.

source: Ye et al. (2021) DL-CDH, novel-query setting
finding: On queries outside the training range, adaptation helped in every case and the CBR system with Siamese retrieval beat the plain regressor. The benefit grew as the query moved further from the training data.
numbers: Training on ages 20-50. Test under 20: regressor 8.95, Siamese+adapt 8.09, L1+adapt 9.18. Test 50-70: regressor 15.51, Siamese+adapt 12.02, L1+adapt 14.74. Test over 70: regressor 32.77, Siamese+adapt 28.83, L1+adapt 32.11. Adaptation always lowered error versus retrieval alone here (over 70: 33.05 to 28.83).
limits: Single dataset, 10-fold protocol. Gains in years of error are modest in absolute terms. Compared against one regressor architecture only.
agent_relevance: Edit-from-neighbour beats direct prediction mainly when the query is novel. That supports using retrieve-and-edit for out-of-pattern problems and plain solving for familiar ones.

source: Ye et al. (2021) DL-CDH, retrieval-adaptation mismatch
finding: The paper reports a mismatch effect: retrieval and adaptation trained independently can be out of step. The adaptation net is trained on random pairs that differ a lot, so it is not tuned for the small differences between a query and its best match. Adaptation-guided retrieval or alternating optimisation (Leake and Ye 2021) is named as the remedy.
numbers: Only Siamese+adapt in the normal setting got worse after adaptation (7.49 to 7.86 years).
quote: Because retrieval and adaptation are trained independently, the two stages may be out of synchronization.
limits: Explanation is the authors' reading; not tested in this paper by an intervention.
agent_relevance: Choose what to retrieve by how editable it is, not by raw similarity alone. For the agent, rank candidate precedents by how small and checkable the needed edit is.

source: Hanney and Keane (1996) Learning adaptation rules from a case-base (as described in Ye et al. 2021 and d'Aquin et al. 2007)
finding: Origin of the case difference heuristic. Pairs of similar cases are formed. The difference between their problems predicts the difference between their solutions. Rules are learned from these pairs and can be merged when conditions and effects are alike.
numbers: Second-hand: tested on flat/house price estimation and servo rise time; the CBR system with learned adaptation performed better than without adaptation (as reported by d'Aquin et al. 2007).
limits: I did not open the original; numbers not seen. Domains are numeric regression where difference-addition is natural.
agent_relevance: The pair-difference idea turns past solved problems into edit rules without hand writing. For text problems the 'difference' must be a typed edit, not free text.

source: d'Aquin, Badra, Lafrogne, Lieber, Napoli, Szathmary (2006) Adaptation knowledge discovery from a case base (CABAMAKA)
finding: CABAMAKA extends Hanney and Keane by looking at every ordered pair of cases, not only similar ones, and mines frequent closed itemsets (CHARM algorithm) from pair differences. A human analyst interprets the itemsets as adaptation rules and writes an explanation for each.
numbers: Breast cancer treatment domain, n about 750 cases, so about 5x10^5 ordered pairs.
quote: Adaptation is modelled as a transformation: problem difference, then adaptation knowledge, then solution difference, then edited solution.
limits: Short conference paper; no quantitative performance test. Analyst validation required.
agent_relevance: Shows an adaptation rule can be stored with its explanation and human validation. For the agent, a learned edit rule should carry its reason and be validated by test before reuse.

source: d'Aquin, Badra, Lafrogne, Lieber, Napoli, Szathmary (2007) Case base mining for adaptation knowledge acquisition
finding: Full version of CABAMAKA. Gives the three-step adaptation model (srce,tgt) to pb, (pb,AK) to sol, (Sol(srce),sol) to Sol(tgt), and the property notation =, -, + for kept, lost, gained properties. Lists related AKA methods: DIAL adaptation cases (Leake 1996), Jarmulak adaptation case base (2001), Shiu fuzzy trees (2001), Wiratunga C4.5 on adaptation cases (2002).
numbers: n = 647 cases, support threshold 10 percent: 2344 frequent closed itemsets in about 2 minutes; 208 kept after requiring a +/- in both problem and solution. One rule shown: tumor under 4 cm in source and over 4 cm in target means swap partial mastectomy for radical mastectomy.
quote: More substantial experiments have to be carried out for an effective evaluation.
limits: Authors admit the evaluation is anecdotal. 208 candidate rules still need an expert to sort.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean typed-edit vocabulary: keep / drop / add. The agent can express an adaptation as such a set diff over solution parts, which code can check.

source: Leake, Kinley, Wilson (1996) DIAL: adaptation cases (as described in d'Aquin et al. 2007)
finding: DIAL, a disaster-response planner, adapts by retrieving an adaptation case: a record of an earlier adaptation as transformations (add, delete, substitute) plus the memory search needed to find the filler. Principle: adaptation equals transformations plus memory search. The record keeps the context, the derivation and the effort spent.
numbers: Second-hand description only; no results seen.
limits: Original not opened.
agent_relevance: Keep a library of past EDITS, not only past solutions. Reuse an earlier edit and the search it needed. That is a retained case of type 'edit' for O7.

source: Jarmulak, Craw, Rowe (2001) adaptation case base for tablet formulation (as described in d'Aquin et al. 2007)
finding: For every case, retrieve its nearest neighbour from the rest of the base and store an adaptation case (the problem difference and the solution difference). Later adaptation is itself case-based on these adaptation cases. Wiratunga et al. (2002) induce general rules from them with C4.5.
numbers: Second-hand; success reported in tablet formulation design, no numbers seen.
limits: Original not opened.
agent_relevance: Leave-one-out construction of edit examples is cheap and needs no new data. Candidate for building an edit library from the agent's own past solved items.

source: Smyth and Keane (1998) Adaptation-guided retrieval: questioning the similarity assumption in reasoning
finding: Argues retrieval should pick the case that is cheapest to adapt, not the most similar (title and d'Aquin et al. mention 'only adaptable cases are retrieved'). Similarity is a poor stand-in for usefulness.
numbers: Only bibliographic data confirmed (127 citations on Crossref); results not seen.
limits: Paywalled; not opened. No number claims recorded.
agent_relevance: Core design rule for the agent: retrieve by 'how editable' not 'how similar'. Rank precedents by estimated edit size and edit certainty.

source: Smyth and Keane (1995) Experiments on adaptation-guided retrieval in case-based design
finding: Earlier ICCBR experiments on the same idea in case-based design. Not read.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Paywalled; not opened.
agent_relevance: Same as above; replication target.

source: Leake and Ye (2021) Harmonizing case retrieval and adaptation with alternating optimization (as described in Ye et al. 2021)
finding: Shows the retrieval and adaptation components drift apart when trained alone and proposes alternating optimisation so each is trained against the other's output.
numbers: Not seen; 10 citations on Crossref.
limits: Paywalled; not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports tuning retrieval and edit steps jointly, which for us means evaluating edit success on the cases retrieval actually returns.

source: Leake et al. (2021) NN-CDH (as described in Ye et al. 2021)
finding: Neural-network CDH predicts solution differences for regression. Per the DL-CDH paper, it performed worse than a regressor in an easy domain but better in a domain with novel queries. Same pattern as DL-CDH.
numbers: Second-hand through Ye et al.; no numbers from original.
limits: Original not opened; claim is Ye et al.'s summary.
agent_relevance: Same pattern in two papers: retrieve-and-edit helps for novel queries, loses to direct learning when data is dense.

source: Wetzel et al. (2020) siamese difference prediction (as described in Ye et al. 2021)
finding: A Siamese network predicts target-value difference for a pair of points and adds it to the known point's value, averaged over an ensemble of points. This is close to CDH in spirit.
numbers: Not seen.
limits: Described only in Ye et al.
agent_relevance: The 'predict the delta from a nearby solved item' idea has independent origin in deep learning.

source: Review of Case-Based Reasoning for LLM Agents: Theoretical Foundations, Architectural Components, and Cognitive Integration (2025)
finding: Proposes that an LLM carries out adaptation as three steps: select useful parts of retrieved solutions, transform them to the target constraints, compose them. Names three modes: transformational (substitute, delete, insert), compositional (merge parts of several cases), generative (LLM writes a new solution guided by cases). Says a meta-process should choose among them.
numbers: Conceptual framework with equations; no new measured results. Its summary table rates adaptation capacity of CBR-LLM as 'Moderate'.
quote: A(q,Cq) = Acompose o Atransform o Aselect(q,Cq)
limits: Position paper. Describes DS-Agent, CBR-RAG and CaseGPT but does not test adaptation modes against each other.
agent_relevance: Gives a vocabulary for O7 (select, transform, compose) but no evidence which mode works. Treat as design menu only [D].

source: Guo et al. (2024) DS-Agent: Automated data science by empowering LLMs with case-based reasoning
finding: A deployment stage that retrieves one past solved data-science task and has the LLM adapt its code (an Adapter prompt) beat zero-shot and one-shot with a random case. The one-pass rate rose sharply, and cost per run fell more than 90 percent versus the full development loop.
numbers: 18 deployment tasks, 10 runs each. One-pass rate with DS-Agent: GPT-3.5 85 percent, GPT-4 about 99 percent (99.44); best baseline 56 percent (GPT-3.5) and 60 percent (GPT-4). Mixtral-8x7B: about 25 points over zero-shot. Cost per run $0.0045 (GPT-3.5) and $0.135 (GPT-4), 92.5 and 91.5 percent less than development stage.
limits: Mixtral-based DS-Agent was still weaker than GPT-3.5/GPT-4 and in Table 3 had worse mean metric than zero-shot on several tasks. One-shot with a random case did not beat zero-shot for GPT-3.5 (an exception the authors note). Tasks are Kaggle-style; solutions only retrieved from the 12 development tasks' output.
agent_relevance: Strong LLM evidence that edit-from-one-retrieved-precedent beats both no precedent and a random precedent. The random-case control shows retrieval quality matters, not just having an example.

source: DS-Agent (2024) ablations: retrieval count and revision from feedback
finding: More retrieved cases HURT the deployment stage: authors say adapting a single example is the design, and extra cases add interference. Removing the revise-from-execution-feedback step (ReviseRank) hurt the development stage, and learning from text insights was worse than learning from a full past case.
numbers: Hyper-parameter study (Fig. 6b) varies number of example cases with GPT-3.5; mean rank worsens as cases increase (figure was garbled in extraction; direction only). Development stage: k=5 retrieved, 5 iterations, 5 debug steps; GPT-4 reaches 100 percent success on 12 tasks.
quote: the presence of more than one example case in the context introduces interference information
limits: Figure values were not recoverable from the text extraction; only direction is reported here.
agent_relevance: One precedent, edited, with real execution feedback, beats many precedents in context. Matches G2 and supports 'edit one, not blend many' as the default for O7.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Memento stores past trajectories as cases (state, action, reward) and reuses them as planner context, with a non-parametric (similarity) or parametric (learned Q-function) case selector. Case memory added a consistent gain on top of a planner-executor agent and on out-of-distribution sets.
numbers: GAIA validation 87.88 percent Pass@3 (GPT-4.1 planner, o3 executor), test 79.40 percent. DeepResearcher: 66.6 F1 / 80.4 PM. Out-of-distribution gains 4.7 to 9.6 absolute points. Component ablation: CBR adds HLE +4.5 F1/+7.0 PM, SimpleQA +3.7/+5.3, DeepResearcher +6.7/+8.2.
limits: Memento reuses cases as context and does not isolate an adaptation step. The authors note possible data contamination on the DeepResearcher sets. Agent is complex, so gains are not attributable to adaptation alone.
agent_relevance: Evidence that retained trajectories help an agent without training. Because the model edits them implicitly, adaptation quality is not separately measured.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: number of retrieved cases K
finding: Performance rose up to K=4 retrieved cases and then plateaued or fell. The authors say a small curated memory works better, unlike few-shot prompting where more examples often help.
quote: performance improves up to K = 4 ... but plateaus or slightly declines for larger K
limits: Gains beyond K=1 are small (under 1 point); no confidence intervals given.
agent_relevance: A second source (with DS-Agent) saying a few precedents suffice. Setting the default to 1 to 4 precedents saves tokens (G7).

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: ablation of planning vs case memory
finding: Without planning, tool use alone can hurt. Case-based memory gave steady additive gains on top of planning.
numbers: Offline executor to online executor (no planner): DeepResearcher -18.0 F1 / -2.1 PM, SimpleQA +28.8/+63.3, HLE +4.8/+7.1. Adding planning: HLE +11.0/+1.6, SimpleQA +32.5/+4.9, DeepResearcher +29.1/+11.5.
limits: Contamination suspected for DeepResearcher benchmarks per the authors.
agent_relevance: Ranks the contributions: decomposition first, case reuse smaller but consistent. Matches a schema where retrieval of cases is one operator among several.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) TextBFGS: case-based reasoning for code optimization via error-operator retrieval
finding: Instead of retrieving whole past solutions, TextBFGS stores abstract 'error to operator' pairs (a diagnosis and a general fix rule) and retrieves by the current error, then asks the LLM to apply the operator to the current code. It is an adaptation-rule library, like Hanney and Keane rules but in text.
numbers: Hard subsets where Qwen3-235B-A22B failed pass@1: HumanEval-Hard 45 tasks, MBPP-Hard 117 tasks. Abstract: +20.5 percent pass (MBPP), -50.6 percent tokens (HumanEval) versus TextGrad-based approaches. Plus pass rate on MBPP-Hard: TextGrad 48.72, TextGrad-Momentum 58.12, with case base up to 78.63.
limits: Table layout was garbled in extraction; method-to-number mapping was reconstructed and may be partly wrong. Only hard subsets where the model failed once. Preprint; authors are not independent of the method.
agent_relevance: Retaining abstract edit operators keyed on the failure signal, not whole solutions, is a candidate form for O7's edit library, and fits G2 (retrieve by the real failing output).

source: Zhang et al. (2026) TextBFGS: cross-domain transfer of retrieval by problem versus by error
finding: Retrieval keyed on problem text overfits surface features and collapses when the case base comes from another domain. Retrieval keyed on the error signal transfers.
numbers: Problem-based retrieval, MBPP tasks with HumanEval case base: Plus pass falls to 58.12 versus 78.63 with MBPP's own case base (a 20.51 point drop), barely above the 48.72 no-case-base baseline. Error-based retrieval cross-domain: HumanEval target with MBPP case base 93.33 Plus (vs 82.22 without case base).
quote: TextBFGS ... outperforms TextBFGS-REMO by +16.24% on the Plus
limits: Same garbled tables as above (the MBPP cross-domain error-based cell reads 74.36, equal to its in-domain cell, which looks suspicious); authors' own method comparison, one model family.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: retrieved edit operators generalise across domains only if indexed by the failure type, not by topic. Index edits by what failed.

source: Nguyen, Moen, Marttinen (2026) CBR-to-SQL: retrieve structure, then revise entities
finding: Splits retrieval-augmented text-to-SQL into a Proposal step (retrieve top-5 masked SQL skeletons and draft SQL) and a Revision step (look up the entities in the database and let the LLM fix the draft to match the schema). The Revision step carries most of the gain.
numbers: MIMICSQL in the CDB setup: full 0.894 execution accuracy / 0.862 logical form; without Revision 0.786 / 0.776 (-10.8 points); replacing Proposal with ordinary RAG retrieval 0.889 / 0.851. Knowledge base shrunk from 8,000 to 774 (MIMICSQL) and 5,000 to 492 (EHRSQL) by clustering masked skeletons. Condition-value accuracy +2.9 (MIMICSQL) and +4.0 (EHRSQL) over RAG-to-SQL.
limits: Single domain (clinical SQL). Preprint under review. Revision uses a lookup table the authors built; benefit may depend on it. Masked retrieval added little (0.005 execution accuracy).
agent_relevance: Direct LLM evidence that a separate, grounded revision step after reuse matters more than retrieval refinement: the edit step is where the specific entities get fixed against ground truth. Supports an explicit O7 stage with a lookup/check.

source: Nguyen et al. (2026) CBR-to-SQL: robustness
finding: The two-stage design degraded more gracefully than ordinary RAG when the case base was cut or retrieval perturbed. Brittleness was lower.
numbers: Brittleness (lower better), execution: MIMICSQL RAG-to-SQL 0.082 vs CBR-to-SQL 0.065; EHRSQL 0.171 vs 0.086. Logical form: 0.079 vs 0.061 (MIMICSQL) and 0.184 vs 0.182 (EHRSQL, almost no change).
limits: On EHRSQL logical form the brittleness difference is 0.002, i.e. none. Authors' own metric.
agent_relevance: Decoupling 'what shape' from 'which values' reduces brittleness. A scaffold can edit structure first, then bind specifics.

source: Sourati, Ilievski, Sommerauer (2023) Case-based reasoning with language models for classification of logical fallacies
finding: A trained adapter (multi-head attention, 8 heads) fuses a new argument with retrieved similar cases before a classifier. This is learned adaptation of cases for a classification task. It helped three small LMs in-domain and out-of-domain and beat few-shot Codex with 13 examples.
numbers: LOGIC (in-domain) weighted F1, CBR vs baseline: RoBERTa 0.657 vs 0.599; BERT 0.619 vs 0.560; ELECTRA 0.611 vs 0.586. LOGIC Climate (out-of-domain): RoBERTa 0.270 vs 0.217; BERT 0.245 vs 0.200; ELECTRA 0.200 vs 0.120. Gains 2.5 to 6 F1 points in-domain and up to 8 out-of-domain. Best at k=1 with 10 percent of the case base. Rare classes: Equivocation 0 to 0.35, Fallacy of Extension 0.48 to 0.75.
quote: outperforms the vanilla baselines by 2.5 - 6 absolute F1 points on the in-domain dataset
limits: Row labels in the extracted table are scrambled; model-to-row mapping is my reading and the text says ELECTRA is best, which does not fit it. Small LMs trained on augmented, balanced data (281 per class). Out-of-domain F1 stays low (0.20 to 0.27).
agent_relevance: Best at k=1 and with a small case base again: one close precedent, not many. Gains are biggest where data is thin, so reuse matters most for rare problem types.

source: Wilkerson and Leake (2024) On implementing case-based reasoning with large language models
finding: ICCBR 2024 paper from the Leake group on how LLMs can fill CBR roles, including adaptation. Cited 25 times (Crossref). I could not open it.
numbers: Not seen.
limits: Paywalled; abstract not obtained. Do not rely on any claim.
agent_relevance: Follow-up target for Angle B or C: how the field's main adaptation group uses LLMs as the adapter.

source: Pointers: Lopez de Mantaras et al. (2005); Kolodner (1993) Case-Based Reasoning; Wilke and Bergmann (1998) techniques and knowledge for adaptation
finding: Standard references named by Ye et al. (2021) for the CBR cycle and for adaptation kinds (substitution, transformation, generative re-derivation). Not read this session; recorded so later angles can cover them.
numbers: None recorded.
limits: Not opened. Treated as pointers, not evidence.
agent_relevance: Citation trail for a later pass.

source: Badra, Cordier, Lieber (2009) Opportunistic adaptation knowledge discovery (Taaable)
finding: Adaptation knowledge is discovered at problem-solving time. When a recipe adaptation fails or needs refinement, the system mines the case base for ingredient substitutions (e.g. peanut oil to olive oil) with support above a threshold, shows each to the user with the corrected recipe, and stores it if the user accepts.
numbers: Case base 862 recipes (CCC 2008). Mining by frequent closed itemsets over variations between recipe pairs. Feasibility shown on use cases only; no accuracy figures.
limits: Prototype; the authors state more extensive testing is future work. Human validates each substitution.
agent_relevance: Edit rules mined on demand, triggered by a failure and validated before storing, match G1 and G2: search for a repair only after a check fails. A code validator can replace the human in our setting.

source: Taaable opportunistic AK discovery: relation to CHEF and DIAL
finding: The authors compare their method with DIAL (adaptation cases, interactive and opportunistic) and CHEF (learns causal failure explanations so the same failure is not repeated) and say they go one step further by turning failures into knowledge usable more widely.
numbers: Qualitative comparison.
limits: Authors' positioning; not an empirical comparison.
agent_relevance: Two routes to learning from failure: specific (CHEF, avoid this failure) and general (mine substitution rules). A schema could keep both: failure notes and edit rules.

source: Synthesis across opened sources: what is measured for adaptation as a separate step
finding: Only a few papers isolate the edit step with an ablation: CBR-to-SQL (Revision removal -10.8 execution points), DS-Agent (ReviseRank removal worse), DL-CDH (adaptation vs retrieval alone: better in 7 of 8 conditions, worse in 1). Most LLM systems (Memento, fallacy adapter) measure case use as a whole.
numbers: DL-CDH had 8 retrieval/adaptation pairs (2 retrieval methods x 4 test settings); adaptation lowered error in 7. CBR-to-SQL: 0.894 to 0.786.
limits: This is my tally, not a published meta-analysis. Different tasks and metrics. Selection bias: papers that add an edit step report it helping.
agent_relevance: The key gap for us: no found study compares an LLM edit of a retrieved solution against a fresh attempt at equal tokens. This is the test named in SUBFIELDS.md (point 3).
